A mom has opened up about the rare condition that means her toddler has a permanent "mask-like face" that stops him from forming expressions. Following a textbook pregnancy without any concerns, Jeannie Hochstetler of Indiana welcomed her first child on January 29, 2025. She told Newsweek that there were "no concerns" ahead of her son’s birth, and the only sign of anything unusual was that her stomach measured small. At the time, Hochstetler, 28, believed she was having a small baby, which is not uncommon. However, it quickly became evident that something was wrong following Riley’s birth. Read More on Family & Parenting ... "He did not cry when he was born and I assumed he needed a little support adjusting to the outside world," Hochstetler said. "They whisked him away and placed oxygen on him. I remember the doctor standing above him with his chin in his hand for what seemed like hours. Looking back, I realize he knew something was wrong, he just didn’t know what." Riley was transferred to the local NICU ward at a hospital 40 minutes away. Further assessment revealed that Riley has small, webbed hands, and is also missing his right pectoral muscle. Additionally, doctors were unable to open his mouth very far, so Riley was placed on CPAP and given an NG tube for feeding. Nevertheless, Riley "remained a mystery" as doctors struggled to diagnose him. He remained in the NICU for weeks as his condition was assessed. Ultimately, one of the doctors in the ward suggested that Riley could have Poland-Moebius Syndrome, a rare congenital condition that causes facial paralysis and underdeveloped chest muscles. Given the complexities of Poland-Moebius Syndrome, Riley was transferred to a larger NICU three hours away. "This was one of the hardest parts for me. I was two weeks postpartum, watching strangers load my baby into a helicopter—what a wild introduction to parenthood," Hochstetler said. ... At three weeks old, Riley was officially diagnosed with Poland-Moebius Syndrome. The 'National Institutes of Health (NIH) suggests that Moebius Syndrome occurs in an estimated one per 50,000 live births, causing the underdevelopment of facial nerves that control expressions and eye movements. People with Moebius Syndrome can experience trouble swallowing, difficulties with speech, inability to smile or frown, hearing problems and motor delays. Poland syndrome is often linked to Moebius Syndrome, leading to missing or underdeveloped chest muscles. It was a whirlwind moment when Hochstetler was told her son’s diagnosis. She had never heard of either condition, so there was a lot of uncertainty about Riley’s future. She said: "Hearing that my baby would never smile at me was one of the hardest parts. I remember feeling grief because this was not the parenthood I envisioned. I also felt sadness for my baby and all the things he had already endured and would have to endure. "We were told that each case of Moebius is different, and we would just have to wait and see how severely Riley was affected. They told us he would not be able to form facial expressions or blink, he would have difficulty feeding, and he would be delayed with milestones." There is no cure for Moebius Syndrome, so the family can only treat the symptoms and manage Riley’s condition. Riley is missing his seventh cranial nerve, which is responsible for facial movement and he has restricted eye movement. However, he has continued to adapt and conveys his emotions in a variety of other ways. Riley uses a G-tube for feeding, but Hochstetler hopes to introduce oral feedings when his swallow gets stronger. "He has also had a strabismus surgery done at 13 months old to correct his crossed eyes," she explained. "At the same time he also had a surgery performed to fix eyelashes that laid on his eyes. He’s had two MRIs done and multiple ABRs (hearing tests). Riley has mild hearing loss in his left ear." ... "He has the best laugh in the world and it’s my favorite sound," Hochstetler told Newsweek . "He also does not hesitate to use his voice when he’s not happy. I’ve also become adept at reading his body language to know what he’s feeling." "His condition is non-progressive, which means what he’s born with won’t get worse. With therapy a lot of things can improve, and they already have. He is so adaptable and clever—he figures out how to do things in his own way. He amazes me," she continued. Following Riley’s diagnosis, Hochstetler has been documenting her family’s experiences on social media (@jeanniebontrager on TikTok) to raise awareness of Moebius Syndrome. Riley has taught her so much about strength and resilience, and Hochstetler hopes to show that love can be shown in so many different ways. Hochstetler said: "He is my biggest blessing, and I am so incredibly thankful to be his mom. He has been through so much in his short life and yet he still is one of the happiest babies." https://www.asiaone.com:443/world/russia.text: world Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes that leave 7 dead, many injured Firefighters put out a fire after a residential building was hit following Russia's drone attack in Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Aug 9, 2026. PHOTO: Associated Press PUBLISHED ON August 10, 2026 2:07 AM KYIV, Ukraine — Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes overnight that killed civilians and injured many others on both sides, local authorities reported. Large-scale Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian cities have become almost routine in recent weeks, with Moscow exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of interceptors for the US-made Patriot systems - the sole air defence weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles. In the latest attacks, Ukrainian drones killed five people and injured two dozen others, including a 4-year-old boy, in Russia's border region of Belgorod, according to the regional administration. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, Russian missiles struck a high-rise apartment block in the Saltivskyi district, killing two people and injuring 13, according to regional head Oleh Syniehubov. Eight more people were injured in Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa after "dozens of missiles and drones" struck the city and surrounding region, according to local administration head Oleh Kiper. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has for months lobbied other countries, especially the US, to send Ukraine more Patriot systems made scarcer by the Iran war, arguing they are crucial for defending civilians. Failing that, Zelenskyy wants to make Patriot ammunition in Ukraine or get approval from Elon Musk to use his Starlink satellite communications system to guide strikes inside Russia that can hit its missile launchers. Meanwhile, Kyiv has kept up long-range drone strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, as well as the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries, and other targets deep inside Russia, sparking a fuel crisis. Russia's defence ministry on Sunday (Aug 9) claimed its overnight strikes hit drone warehouses in the Kharkiv region, as well as fuel depots and stores of other materiel belonging to Ukraine's armed forces at the port of Odesa. It said its forces had shot down 153 Ukrainian drones during the night, including over Russian-occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas. In Russia's Belgorod region, authorities said Ukrainian drone strikes damaged 29 apartment blocks and five private houses, as well as administrative buildings and unspecified "commercial facilities." Debris from Ukrainian drones also fell on two enterprises and a private home in the Russian city of Novorossiysk, mayor Andrey Kravchenko said on Sunday. He did not specify what the commercial sites were. Regional authorities later said falling debris had injured one person, damaged two private houses, and blew out a window in an apartment block. A major fuel terminal is located at Novorossiysk that links Kazakhstan's oil fields to markets around the world, and which has previously been a target for Ukrainian strikes. Moldova says blast near Ukraine border caused by drone A "powerful explosion" believed to be from a combat drone was reported in the village of Crocmaz, in southeast Moldova near the border with Ukraine, local police said Sunday. No one was injured by the impact, which caused a vegetation fire in the Stefan Voda district, police said, adding that "fragments of a combat drone were found at the scene" and would be examined by specialists. Police did not specify the origin of the drone. Multiple drones have violated Moldovan airspace since Russia launched its full-scale war in neighbouring Ukraine. Bulgaria summons Ukrainian ambassador over drone incident Bulgaria has summoned Ukraine's ambassador after a drone entered Bulgarian airspace, the country's public broadcaster BNT reported on Sunday. The drone exploded on Saturday close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania. No casualties or damage were reported. Bulgaria's defence ministry said the drone appeared to be the type used by Ukrainian armed forces, and that the incident was likely accidental. Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said the incident was being examined, but that it did not deliberately target Bulgaria. Ukraine and Bulgaria were in "close contact" to clarify what had happened, he added. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: A social media post by a now former Anthropic employee has sparked discussion about the danger of unregulated AI. Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty Images View image in fullscreen A social media post by a now former Anthropic employee has sparked discussion about the danger of unregulated AI. Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanity Richard Luscombe Wed 9 Sep 2026 20.14 EDT First published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic , one of whom has quit his job in protest. The latest doom-laden predictions came in posts on social media on Tuesday by a researcher who said he resigned because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI , were ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” wrote Jacob Coxon. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them? Read more The post garnered responses from at least two other Anthropic employees who backed up Coxon’s dire predictions. In the first, Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said his former colleague was “correct”, and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote . “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Hubinger’s comments mark a surprising affirmation of Coxon’s unflattering, apocalyptic predictions from a person still on Anthropic’s payroll. A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, who posted a lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity, and not the views of his employer. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Marks. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said. “Anthropic has been a pioneer in mechanistic interpretability, the science of looking inside AI models to understand how they work, which is now being used to analyze and prevent incidents of AI misalignment across the industry. We were the first lab to publish a Responsible Scaling Policy, a public framework dedicated to mitigating catastrophic risks from AI models and we continue to aggressively test our models for dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology, and publish what we learn for scrutiny and research. “This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.” The researchers’ musings on the possibility of human extinction follow more concrete warnings about AI’s cybersecurity capabilities by Sam Altman, chief executive of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has conceded previously that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion Altman said last year that certain aspects of AI, including what he called the “silent surrender” of human decision-making, terrified him. AI executives have shared some concerns about the direction of AI and its growing ability to manipulate, seize and control human functions and actions. A sharp rise was reported this summer in incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways. In one of the most publicized examples, staff at OpenAI recorded rogue behavior among its leading AI agents that escaped a closed training environment in July to access the open web and launch an unprecedented hacking attack on the software repository Hugging Face. OpenAI, the San Francisco-based startup behind the publicly available AI bot ChatGPT, later admitted that it should have responded earlier to warning signals of the days-long attack, which is widely considered to be the first autonomous agent cyber-attack. Those executives, however, have stopped short of agreeing with the full doomsday warnings like Coxon’s and have bristled at any attempts to regulate the AI industry. Some politicians have urged the industry to slow down, or in some cases, halt development on AI altogether. Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, reposted Coxon’s resignation on Wednesday with his own note: “Mr. Coxon is right. The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity.” Sanders said he would soon introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) earlier this month have set off a war of words between North and South Korea By Koh Ewe Â and Â Jake Kwon ,Â Seoul correspondent Published 30 September 2026, 04:38 BST Updated 06:24 BST South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month. Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September. South Korea said on Tuesday it was "certain" that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, came from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what he said was a violation of a decades-old armistice. North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation". Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea. Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making." South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border. South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War. That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas. In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ. In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied. Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now. Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen. Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations". As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015. "Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says. The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms". "UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The Krome detention center in west Miami, Florida, on the Fourth of July in 2025. Photograph: Pedro Portal/Miami Herald via Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Krome detention center in west Miami, Florida, on the Fourth of July in 2025. Photograph: Pedro Portal/Miami Herald via Getty Images Florida Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail Richard Luscombe in Miami Wed 21 Oct 2026 09.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions. Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida. The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days. “I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa ,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference. “We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.” The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE. Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “ Alligator Alcatraz ” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year. “He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare. “Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’ “They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.” Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent. “We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said. Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move. “This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said. “Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.” Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details. Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said. “The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.” During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”. Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space. Advocates say Donald Trump ’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries. The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties. A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival. https://www.texarkanagazette.com/news/20.text: Moscow's secrecy about a suspected plague case follows a pattern from the Soviet era The Kremlin has long maintained a culture of secrecy when it comes to controlling public information, especially involving accidents -- from industrial disasters to health emergencies. The suspicious death last week of a worker at a research lab in Siberia that has fueled global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague is just the latest example of how leaders in Moscow manage the official narrative that often covers up the truth for years. Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, has told the World Health Organization that no case of plague has been registered in the Irkutsk region of southeastern Siberia. In tersely worded statements, the Russian agency said the lab worker contracted pneumonia of "unknown" origin and that tests found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The WHO urged Russia to share more information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures and media reports that a second employee had pneumonia of undetermined cause. Scarce official information about the worker's death, which unconfirmed reports in Russia blamed on pneumonic plague, follows the Soviet-era patterns of secrecy in dealing with outbreaks of infectious diseases, accidents and other emergencies. Here are other examples of Moscow censoring public health information: THE 1959-60 SMALLPOX OUTBREAK In the final days of December 1959, leading Soviet graphic artist Alexei Kokorekin fell ill and died shortly after returning from a trip to India. Doctors initially struggled to identify the cause of death as smallpox, which was considered eradicated decades earlier. Once it became clear, authorities launched a massive effort to contain the outbreak. The KGB meticulously tracked down Kokorekin's contacts, and thousands of people were put in isolation. An Aeroflot flight carrying one of his contacts was contacted before it landed in Paris and ordered to return to Moscow. Authorities halted all travel to and from Moscow and launched an unprecedented effort in which thousands of vaccination teams distributed shots to millions of residents of the capital and the surrounding region. International news outlets reported the massive campaign, but Soviet state media kept silent about it. The outbreak led to 46 confirmed cases and three deaths in Moscow before it was contained in 44 days. A novel and movie based on the outbreak appeared later, but the true details of what happened were hidden from the public until the waning years of the Soviet Union. THE 1971 ARAL SEA SMALLPOX OUTBREAK During tests of a smallpox bioweapon on a tightly guarded range on Vozrozhdeniya Island in the Aral Sea in August 1971, a research ship accidentally sailed too close to the aerosolized plume of microbes. A marine biologist on the ship contracted smallpox and spread it to several others in the town of Aralsk in what is now part of Kazakhstan, resulting in 10 infections and three deaths. The town was quarantined and more than 40,000 people were vaccinated against smallpox within days, but the public remained unaware of what happened. The incident only became widely known in 2002 when U.S. researchers publicized old Soviet archives. The 1979 anthrax leak On April 2, 1979, anthrax spores were accidentally released from a secret biological weapons lab in Sverdlovsk, the Ural Mountains city that is now called Yekaterinburg. The accident was caused by a worker failing to replace a faulty ventilation filter, resulting in the release of the deadly spores into the air. At least 68 people died in the resulting anthrax outbreak. Soviet authorities officially blamed the deaths on contaminated meat from a street market and the KGB made sure to keep details of the accident under wraps, confiscating medical records. It wasn't until after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union that the truth about the outbreak became known under Russian President Boris Yeltsin, a former Communist Party boss in Sverdlovsk. THE 1986 CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR DISASTER When the reactor No. 4 exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in the then-Soviet republic of Ukraine on April 26, 1986, it spewed a radioactive cloud across Europe. Authorities were slow to report the incident and warn the public about the radioactive threat. When Sweden detected the radiation, Moscow initially denied that any accident had occurred. Soviet officials waited for 36 hours before ordering the evacuation of the town of Pripyat near the plant. Five days later, tens of thousands of people were exposed to radioactive fallout as they marched through the streets of Kyiv during the May Day parade. Despite Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of "glasnost," or greater openness, authorities heavily censored medical data and casualty figures as part of their efforts to conceal the true scale of the disaster. Immediately after the accident, 30 plant workers and firefighters died from acute radiation sickness, and thousands of people later died from radiation-related illnesses. THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC During the COVID-19 pandemic, some independent Russian news outlets and international media reports claimed the country's coronavirus death toll could be much higher than government officials said. The reports cited a spike in total mortality rates. Russian authorities angrily rejected the claims as part of a Western disinformation campaign against Moscow. Officials in Moscow explained the relatively low death toll by crediting a swift ban on travel from China early in the pandemic, a speedy introduction of restrictions and a broad testing effort that allowed authorities to spot infections quickly and prevent patients from developing life-threatening complications. Authorities denied claims of widespread shortages of personal protective equipment and questionable infection control procedures at dozens of hospitals. Some medical workers said they were threatened with dismissal or even prosecution for complaining about the situation. In 2020, Russia criminalized "false information" about threats to public safety, and human rights groups documented that dozens of people were prosecuted for making purportedly fake claims. But at the end of that year, officials effectively conceded the death toll was several times higher than previously reported. In early 2022, Russian authorities reported a total of over 13.5 million confirmed COVID-19 and 338,091 deaths -- by far the highest death toll in Europe at the time. Russia's state statistics agency Rosstat, which uses broader counting criteria, said there were 681,100 virus-linked deaths between April 2020 and December 2021. "The system can silence, but it's not competent enough to coordinate, so it produces contradiction instead of a unified false account," Judy Twigg, professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, said in written comments this week. ------ Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed.
